messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sione Tui is a 63-year-old community organizer who has spent most of his adult life walking into tense public spaces and trying to steady them. Last year, on his way home from an evening neighborhood meeting, he was caught in a life-threatening traffic accident when a pickup truck ran a red light and struck the driver’s side of his car hard enough to spin it into a barrier. What remains with him is jagged rather than complete. He can see, with unnerving precision, the wash of headlights across the windshield and the sudden sight of a uniformed officer leaning down near the shattered window, but whole stretches are blank. He says he knows something terrible happened in between, yet when he tries to describe it, words fail him; he stops, shakes his head, and says only that parts are “gone” no matter how hard he reaches for them.

In the weeks after the crash, Sione became preoccupied with how he had behaved in those final seconds before impact. He had come to believe the accident happened because of the way he acted, replaying his decision to keep driving through the intersection and wondering if a more alert, more disciplined man would have avoided it. The worst part for him was not only the fear he had felt then, but the sense now that his own body had betrayed him and kept betraying him afterward. His chest tightens, his muscles brace, and his heart surges in ordinary moments, and he reads these reactions as proof that his body is now an enemy, stuck in danger even when he knows he is in a meeting room or at home. Over time he has also begun to describe himself as feeling dead inside, as if the crash hollowed something out that has not come back.

Those beliefs shape the way he tries to remember. When he sits with the event, he does not approach it with curiosity so much as accusation, searching the blank places for evidence of what he did wrong. The more he tells himself that the accident happened because of his own actions, and that his body’s continuing alarms mean something in him is permanently damaged, the more the memory seems to fracture under him. A few images stand out with painful clarity, while the missing portions feel unreachable; he becomes frustrated, falls silent, and says again that he cannot find words for what happened. The gaps themselves have taken on meaning for him, as if not being able to tell the story properly confirms that something is fundamentally wrong in him.

At the same time, the shape of the memory determines what now feels dangerous. Because one of the clearest surviving images is of a uniform at his car window, police and military uniforms have become especially potent. He notices them immediately on the street, at city buildings, even at public events he helps organize, and in those moments the crash feels less like a past event than something half-returning. The same is true of anger. He cannot fully recall all that was said around the scene, but he retains a vivid sense of sharp voices and command in the aftermath, and now even calm expressions of anger from other people can set his body off. Unwanted thoughts arrive with these reminders, not as a full story but as abrupt flashes and pressure to remember what is missing.

His work has made this especially hard. As a community organizer, he spends his days in church basements, school auditoriums, and municipal meetings where conflict is common and uniformed security or police officers are often present. When a resident speaks angrily at a planning meeting, even in a measured tone, Sione feels his body jolt before he can think. In those moments he becomes certain that his reactions mean he is still broken and unsafe in his own skin. Seeing how strongly he responds also deepens his self-blame: if he were stronger, he thinks, a voice or a uniform would not have this kind of power over him. What frightens him most is that these encounters seem to prove the crash is still inside him.

The cycle has tightened over months. A trigger at work or on the street brings intrusive thoughts and a bodily surge, and Sione reads that surge as evidence that his body cannot be trusted and that he somehow caused lasting damage by how he acted that night. Those conclusions send him back toward the memory, but only in a punishing way, and the result is more blankness, more difficulty putting the event into words, and more fixation on the few sharply lit fragments that make uniforms and anger impossible to ignore. He has become less present with colleagues and more detached with family, not because he does not care, but because feeling “dead inside” seems safer than being caught by another rush of alarm.

He sought help after freezing during a neighborhood mediation when two men began arguing and a uniformed officer stepped into the doorway. Sione lost track of the discussion, felt the old jolt flood his body, and afterward sat in his car unable to explain to a coworker what had happened. He came in frightened that he is becoming a man ruled by fragments, and hoping, quietly, that if he can finally find words for the crash, the world might stop feeling so ready to happen to him again.
